warmup.q: A pool of 4 threads has 10 tasks waiting in its queue, and each task takes 1 second. main calls pool.shutdown() and then prints "done". When does "done" appear?
options: Right away, while the tasks keep running
After about 3 seconds, when the last task finishes
Never, because shutdown() blocks until someone calls awaitTermination()
Right away, and the 10 tasks are cancelled
warmup.why: shutdown() only stops new tasks from coming in. Queued and running tasks carry on, and the call returns at once. Waiting is a separate step: awaitTermination or, since JDK 19, close(). Nothing is cancelled either; that would be shutdownNow(). The third section runs a program much like this one.

opening:
Picture a restaurant with a strange way of hiring. For every order, the manager hires a new cook, who signs a contract, puts on an apron, cooks one dish and goes home. For a slow roast, the paperwork hardly matters. For a side salad, it takes longer than the salad.

Real kitchens hire a team of cooks once and clip each order to a rail. A cook with free hands takes the next ticket. In Java, each cook is a thread, one path of work running beside others in the same program. The team and its rail make a thread pool, and you can get one in a single line.

The traps sit at either end of a pool's life. A failing task can vanish without a trace, and shutdown() sounds final but waits for nothing. Both pass a quick test.

The memory model track asked what one thread sees of another's writes. Now we stop making threads by hand. In this lesson, we'll measure what a thread per task costs, hand tasks to a pool, close it without losing work, and build a small pool ourselves. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a manager who hired a new cook for every order. We measured what that costs, then handed the orders to a pool. We found that submit keeps a failure to itself, that shutdown() locks the door but waits for nothing, and that a forgotten pool's cooks never go home.

Now search your own code for .submit(, and check that something calls get() on each Future it returns. Then search for shutdown(), and make sure an awaitTermination or a close() follows it.

Next, we'll open ThreadPoolExecutor, the class behind the factory methods. When the tickets pile up on the rail, does the pool call in extra cooks, or turn customers away?

sections.h: What a new thread per task costs, and why it has no ceiling
sections.html:
Let's put a price on the manager's hiring habit. A task is a piece of work you hand over to be run. In Java it's usually a Runnable, an object with one method, void run(). Our tasks are tiny: a few nanoseconds of arithmetic each, about the size of one side salad.

The first version gives every task a brand-new thread, just as Threads from zero did with its workers:

Java
// Naive: a brand-new thread for every task
CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks);
for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) {
    new Thread(() -> { task(); done.countDown(); }).start();
}
done.await();                        // returns when every task has counted down
Kotlin
// Naive: a brand-new thread for every task
val done = CountDownLatch(tasks)
repeat(tasks) {
    Thread { task(); done.countDown() }.start()
}
done.await()                         // returns when every task has counted down

done is a CountDownLatch, the one-shot gate from Synchronizers. Each task counts it down once, and await() returns when it reaches zero. The second version runs the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused:

Java
// Fixed: four threads, created once and reused for every task
try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
    for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.execute(ThreadPerTaskDemo::task);
}                                    // close() waits for all of them
Kotlin
// Fixed: four threads, created once and reused for every task
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool ->
    repeat(tasks) { pool.execute(::task) }
}                                    // close() waits for all of them

For now, read newFixedThreadPool(4) as "four cooks and one rail". The rest of this lesson takes that line apart.

My guess before running it: the pool wins, maybe by ten times. ThreadPerTaskDemo, in the Try it below, does 5,000 tasks both ways, twice. It ran on a Linux machine with 4 cores, the parts of the processor that each run one thread at a time. When the machine was quiet, a new thread per task took 0.5 to 1.5 seconds per round, and the pool took 6 to 25 ms. While it was busy with other heavy programs, one run printed:

round 1: 5,000 tasks  new thread each: 2,635 ms  pool of 4: 44 ms
round 2: 5,000 tasks  new thread each: 2,939 ms  pool of 4: 20 ms

Correctness first: both versions ran all 5,000 tasks. Then speed. In this run, the pool was 60 to 150 times faster, far beyond my guess.

The work was identical, so the difference is the threads. An ordinary Java thread is a platform thread: it wraps one thread of the operating system. Starting one is a trip to the kernel, the core of the operating system.

The new thread gets its own stack, the private memory for its local variables and calls in progress. On 64-bit Linux, the JVM (the Java Virtual Machine, the program that runs your compiled code) reserves 1 MB for each stack by default. The thread also gets a place in the scheduler, the part of the operating system that decides which thread runs next.

When the thread ends, all of that is torn down again. Threads from zero measured the round trip at about 130 microseconds. A task that runs for nanoseconds pays thousands of times its own cost just to start.

The second cost hides until the busiest hour. A thread per task has no ceiling. If 3,000 orders arrive at once, you get 3,000 threads. Something runs out first: the operating system's limit on threads, memory for their stacks, or CPU time spent switching between threads that all want a core. In Java, the first sign is often an OutOfMemoryError that says unable to create native thread.

A thread pool fixes both costs. It creates a few threads once and keeps them. Each thread loops: take a task from a queue, run it, take the next one.

In the kitchen, the threads are the cooks, the queue is the rail and the pool size is the number of cooks. The pool size also caps how many tasks run at the same moment. So 3,000 orders become 3,000 tickets on the rail, not 3,000 cooks squeezed into a kitchen with four stoves.

A thread per tiny task costs more than the task. Create threads once, and reuse them.

Virtual threads are much lighter threads that the JVM runs on top of a few platform threads, and the virtual threads track covers them. They make a new thread cheap, so the first cost mostly goes away. The second cost doesn't: you still want a limit on how much work runs at once. With virtual threads, you put that limit on the scarce thing itself, such as the number of calls to a slow service.

So we want a pool. Java has one ready-made, behind two interfaces, and the first trap waits in the difference between two of their methods.

try.title: Pay for 5,000 threads
steps: Predict first: for 5,000 tiny tasks, how many times slower is a new thread per task than a pool of 4? Twice? Ten times? A hundred?
Run ThreadPerTaskDemo (Java or Kotlin, they do the same thing) with the command below. It runs two rounds.
Run it again with -Pargs=10000 added. Does each column double?

code.title: ThreadPerTaskDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ public class ThreadPerTaskDemo { static final LongAdder work = new LongAdder(); static void task() { work.add(Long.toHexString(System.nanoTime()).length()); // a few nanoseconds of real work } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 5_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 2; round++) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task long t0 = System.nanoTime(); CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) { new Thread(() -> { task(); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); long perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.execute(ThreadPerTaskDemo::task); } // close() waits for all of them long pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms%n", round, tasks, perTask, pooled); } } }

alt.title: ThreadPerTaskDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder private val work = LongAdder() private fun task() { work.add(System.nanoTime().toString(16).length.toLong()) // a few nanoseconds of real work } /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tasks = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 5_000 for (round in 1..2) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task var t0 = System.nanoTime() val done = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { Thread { task(); done.countDown() }.start() } done.await() val perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> repeat(tasks) { pool.execute(::task) } } // close() waits for all of them val pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms".format(round, tasks, perTask, pooled)) } }

try.expect: On a quiet 4-core machine, a new thread per task took 0.5 to 1.5 seconds per round and the pool took 6 to 25 ms. A busy machine makes both columns slower. The pool's first round is usually its slowest, because the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into fast machine code, is still warming up. With 10,000 tasks the first column roughly doubles, because every task pays for its own thread. The pool pays for four threads in all.

video.title: A manager who hires a cook for every order: a new thread per tiny task costs more than the task and has no ceiling, a pool hires its cooks once, shutdown only locks the door, and awaitTermination waits

sections.h: Handing tasks to a pool: Executor, ExecutorService, and where a failure goes
sections.html:
java.util.concurrent, the package of concurrency tools in the JDK (the Java Development Kit, Java's standard tools and library), splits a pool's job into two interfaces.

Executor has one method, void execute(Runnable task). It promises only that the task will run, at some point, on some thread. That may be the calling thread, a new thread or a pool, and code that takes an Executor doesn't need to know which. It's the rail seen from the dining room: you clip the ticket on, and who cooks it is the kitchen's business.

ExecutorService extends Executor with what a real pool needs. submit hands over a task and gives you back a Future, a claim ticket you can later trade for the task's result. invokeAll runs a list of tasks and waits for all of them, and invokeAny returns the result of the first one that succeeds.

The lifecycle methods, shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination and (since JDK 19) close, decide when the kitchen closes. Lesson 4 of this track covers Future in depth.

You rarely write an ExecutorService yourself. The Executors class is a factory, a class whose static methods build ready-made pools for you:

Java
ExecutorService fixed  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);             // 8 threads, a queue with no limit
ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();         // 1 thread, tasks run in order
ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool();             // grows without limit, idle threads leave after 60 s
ExecutorService vts    = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task
Kotlin
val fixed  = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)              // 8 threads, a queue with no limit
val single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()          // 1 thread, tasks run in order
val cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()              // grows without limit, idle threads leave after 60 s
val vts    = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()  // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task

The first three are built on one class, ThreadPoolExecutor, with different settings, and lesson 2 of this track takes it apart. The last one is different. It starts a new virtual thread for every task, so it isn't a pool at all.

Now the trap. execute and submit look interchangeable, and they treat a failing task in opposite ways.

SwallowDemo, in the Try it below, sends the same task both ways to a pool with one thread. The task prints its thread's name and then throws an exception, because the kitchen is out of eggs. Before you read the output, guess what each half prints:

--- execute ---
cooking on pool-1-thread-1
Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-1" java.lang.IllegalStateException: out of eggs
    at workbench.executors.l01.SwallowDemo.lambda$main$0(SwallowDemo.java:14)
    ... (three more lines of stack trace)
--- submit ---
cooking on pool-1-thread-2
submit: nothing printed. isDone=true

The kitchen ran out of eggs twice, and only the first time did anyone hear about it.

With execute, the exception escapes the task and ends the worker thread. Every thread has an UncaughtExceptionHandler, the method the JVM calls when an exception escapes a thread, and the default one prints the stack trace. The pool then starts a new worker to replace the one that died. That's why the second task runs on pool-1-thread-2, in a pool of one.

With submit, the pool wraps your task in a FutureTask, a task with a slot for its result. The FutureTask catches the exception and keeps it inside the Future. Nothing is printed. The only way to see the failure is to call get() on the Future, which throws an ExecutionException with your exception as its cause. If nobody ever calls get(), the failure is gone.

submit keeps a task's failure inside its Future. Call get(), or use execute.

So choose on purpose. Use execute for work that nobody waits for, so that a failure at least reaches the handler. Use submit when some code will call get() and deal with the answer. Lesson 9 of this track shows how to log failures from both.

We can hand work to a pool now. What we can't do yet is close it, and closing time has a trap of its own.

try.title: Lose an exception on purpose
steps: Run SwallowDemo below and read the thread name printed for each half.
Delete the whole --- get --- part (the println and the try block around f.get()). Predict: will any trace of the second failure remain?

code.title: SwallowDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ public class SwallowDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Runnable cook = () -> { System.out.println("cooking on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); throw new IllegalStateException("out of eggs"); }; System.out.println("--- execute ---"); pool.execute(cook); Thread.sleep(200); // give the stack trace time to print System.out.println("--- submit ---"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(cook); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone()); System.out.println("--- get ---"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } } }

alt.title: SwallowDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> val cook = Runnable { println("cooking on " + Thread.currentThread().name) throw IllegalStateException("out of eggs") } println("--- execute ---") pool.execute(cook) Thread.sleep(200) // give the stack trace time to print println("--- submit ---") val f = pool.submit(cook) Thread.sleep(200) println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone) println("--- get ---") try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.cause) } } }

try.expect: The first run prints a stack trace for the execute failure. Then the submit task runs on pool-1-thread-2, because the first worker died and the pool replaced it. The get() block prints the ExecutionException and its cause, out of eggs. Without that block, the second failure leaves no trace at all: the exception sits inside a Future that nobody reads.

sections.h: Closing time: shutdown(), shutdownNow() and the wait you must ask for
sections.html:
A restaurant can close in two ways. The gentle way: lock the front door, but cook every order that is already on the rail. The hard way: lock the door, hand the waiting tickets back to the customers, and tell the cooks to stop what they're doing. Either way, someone has to stay until the last cook leaves before turning off the lights.

An ExecutorService has the same choices. It moves through its life one way only: from running, to shutting down or stopping, to terminated. The figure draws the trip. Two methods start it, and neither of them waits.

shutdown() is the gentle close. New tasks are rejected with a RejectedExecutionException. Tasks in the queue and tasks already running carry on. The method returns at once.

ShutdownDemo, in the Try it below, puts that to the test. Two cooks (a pool of two threads) get six orders, and each order takes 300 ms. Then main calls shutdown(), tries to add a seventh order and waits with awaitTermination, which we'll meet in a moment.

My prediction: shutdown() returns within a few milliseconds, long before the first order is cooked. Here's a run (the clock starts with the program, so the first line includes starting the pool):

  115 ms  shutdown returned. isShutdown=true isTerminated=false
  164 ms  order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed
  400 ms  cooked order 1
  403 ms  cooked order 2
  700 ms  cooked order 3
  704 ms  cooked order 4
 1002 ms  cooked order 5
 1005 ms  cooked order 6
 1007 ms  awaitTermination returned true. isTerminated=true

The prediction held. shutdown() returned before a single order was cooked, and the seventh order was turned away. The six orders on the rail were still cooked, two at a time, 300 ms apart.

shutdownNow() is the hard close. It takes every task that hasn't started out of the queue and returns them as a List<Runnable>, so you can see what was never done. Then it interrupts the threads that are running tasks.

An interrupt is a polite request to stop. It sets a flag on the thread, and a thread blocked in sleep, wait or a queue's take wakes up with an InterruptedException. A task busy in a loop that never checks the flag keeps running. (The lesson A thread's life, in the threads track, covered the flag, and lesson 4 of this track comes back to it.)

Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real cook hears "stop!" when you shout it. A Java task hears an interrupt only if it checks for one, or waits in a method that does.

Run the demo with now, and it calls shutdownNow() 100 ms in:

  130 ms  order 2 interrupted
  131 ms  shutdownNow returned 4 tasks that never started
  131 ms  order 1 interrupted
  217 ms  order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed
  223 ms  awaitTermination returned true. isTerminated=true

Orders 1 and 2 were asleep in their 300 ms of cooking, so the interrupt woke them. The pool handed back the four tickets that never started, and nothing was cooked. The interrupted orders print from their own threads, so their lines can land before or after main's line about shutdownNow.

The waiting is a separate call. awaitTermination(timeout, unit) blocks until the pool has terminated or the timeout runs out, and returns true or false to say which. Put the three calls together and you get the shutdown idiom from the ExecutorService documentation (the timeouts are yours to choose):

Java
pool.shutdown();                                         // 1. no new work
try {
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {  // 2. let the backlog finish
        pool.shutdownNow();                              // 3. interrupt the stragglers
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS))
            System.err.println("pool did not terminate");
    }
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    pool.shutdownNow();                                  // we were interrupted: stop now
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();                  // and keep the flag for our caller
}
Kotlin
pool.shutdown()                                          // 1. no new work
try {
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {  // 2. let the backlog finish
        pool.shutdownNow()                               // 3. interrupt the stragglers
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS))
            System.err.println("pool did not terminate")
    }
} catch (e: InterruptedException) {
    pool.shutdownNow()                                   // we were interrupted: stop now
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt()                   // and keep the flag for our caller
}

First we lock the door. Then we give the backlog 20 seconds. If that isn't enough, we interrupt the stragglers and give them 5 more. The catch covers our own thread being interrupted while it waits. Then we stop the pool at once, and set our interrupt flag again so that our caller still sees it.

Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so Java's try-with-resources (Kotlin's use) can do the waiting. close() calls shutdown() and then waits until every task has finished. If the waiting thread is interrupted, it calls shutdownNow(), keeps waiting, and sets the interrupt flag again before it returns.

There's no timeout, so close() waits forever on a task that never ends. Use close() for a short-lived pool inside one method. Use the idiom for a pool that must stop within a deadline.

Forget both, and you meet the most loyal cooks in town. The threads of newFixedThreadPool are not daemon threads, the background helpers that the JVM doesn't wait for. The JVM keeps running until every non-daemon thread has ended. So after main returns, the pool's cooks stand by the empty rail, waiting for orders that will never come, and the program never exits.

shutdown() returns before the work is done. Wait with awaitTermination() or close().

We've used the pool from the outside. Inside, it's smaller than you might think: small enough to build in the lab.

try.title: Watch shutdown not wait
steps: ShutdownDemo gives two cooks (a pool of two threads) six orders of 300 ms each, then calls shutdown(). Predict the time on the shutdown returned line, then run it.
Run it again with -Pargs=now, which calls shutdownNow() after 100 ms instead. Predict how many orders get cooked.

code.title: ShutdownDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a kitchen of 2 cooks (threads) with 6 orders of 300 ms each. */ public class ShutdownDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static Runnable cook(int id) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); // 300 ms to cook one order log("cooked order " + id); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("order " + id + " interrupted"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean now = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("now"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) pool.execute(cook(i)); if (now) { Thread.sleep(100); List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); log("shutdownNow returned " + neverStarted.size() + " tasks that never started"); } else { pool.shutdown(); log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=" + pool.isShutdown() + " isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } try { pool.execute(cook(7)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { log("order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed"); } boolean done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); log("awaitTermination returned " + done + ". isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } }

alt.title: ShutdownDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun cook(id: Int) = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(300) // 300 ms to cook one order log("cooked order $id") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("order $id interrupted") Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a kitchen of 2 cooks (threads) with 6 orders of 300 ms each. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val now = args.firstOrNull() == "now" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2) for (i in 1..6) pool.execute(cook(i)) if (now) { Thread.sleep(100) val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() log("shutdownNow returned ${neverStarted.size} tasks that never started") } else { pool.shutdown() log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=${pool.isShutdown} isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") } try { pool.execute(cook(7)) } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { log("order 7 rejected: the kitchen is closed") } val done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) log("awaitTermination returned $done. isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") }

try.expect: With shutdown(), that line prints a few milliseconds after the pool starts, order 7 is rejected, and the six orders are cooked in pairs, about 300 ms apart. Only then does awaitTermination return true. With now, orders 1 and 2 are interrupted in their sleep, shutdownNow hands back the 4 orders that never started, nothing is cooked, and the pool terminates soon after. The two interrupted lines can come before or after the shutdownNow returned line, because each one prints from its own thread.

aside.title: What happens when a real service is told to stop?
aside.html: If you write web services, programs that answer requests over the network, you'll meet this every time a new version goes out. The system that runs a service usually stops it in two steps: first a polite signal, then, after a grace period, a hard kill. Thirty seconds is a common default. That grace period is your shutdown budget: stop taking new requests, call shutdown(), wait with awaitTermination for most of the budget, then call shutdownNow() and log what it hands back. The framework your service is built on closes the pools it created, and the pools you create yourself are yours to close.

sections.h: Inside a pool: a queue and a few threads that loop
sections.html:
Strip away the options, and a fixed pool is a rail and a few cooks. Each worker thread runs one loop:

Java
while (true) {
    Runnable task = queue.take();   // blocks while the queue is empty
    if (task == POISON) return;     // shutdown: time to go home
    task.run();
}
Kotlin
while (true) {
    val task = queue.take()          // blocks while the queue is empty
    if (task === POISON) return      // shutdown: time to go home
    task.run()
}

execute puts the task on a BlockingQueue, the queue from Concurrent collections whose take() waits while the queue is empty, and the workers take tasks off it. The queue does the hand-off between threads, and the number of workers limits how many tasks run at once.

Shutdown is the interesting part. Idle workers are blocked inside take(), so the pool has to wake them somehow.

Classic problems closed the kitchen at the end of the threads track with a poison pill: a special ticket that means "go home". One pill per cook goes on the rail, behind every real order, and a worker that takes a pill exits. The queue is first in, first out, so every task submitted before shutdown() runs before any worker sees a pill.

shutdownNow() drains the queue instead and puts fresh pills on it. Then it interrupts the workers, so idle ones fall out of take() and busy ones get the request to stop.

There's one race to get right. It has the check-then-act shape from Race conditions: why count++ lies, where another thread can change things between the check and the act. execute checks the shutdown flag, then queues the task. Let's trace two threads:

  1. A waiter's thread calls execute, reads the flag and finds the kitchen open.
  2. Before it queues its ticket, the manager's thread calls shutdown(), sets the flag and puts the pills on the rail.
  3. The waiter's thread queues its ticket, behind the pills.

The waiter was told the order was accepted, and no cook will ever take it. So execute and shutdown() take the same lock, and the check and the queueing happen as one step.

ThreadPoolExecutor solves the same problem another way. It keeps one AtomicInteger called ctl, and packs the run state into its top 3 bits and the worker count into the other 29. That way a single compare-and-set (an update that succeeds only if nobody changed the value first, from Atomics and compare-and-set) can check and change both at once.

The lab uses a plain synchronized lock instead. A lock is slower and far easier to read, which is the right trade when the goal is to see the moving parts.

Check yourself before the lab. The toy pool has four workers, and shutdown() puts one pill on the rail instead of four. What happens?

(One worker takes the pill and exits. The other three stay blocked in take() forever, so awaitTermination returns false. They aren't daemon threads, so the JVM never exits either.)

That's all a fixed pool is. Notice what it lacks, though.

Its rail has no end, so on a busy evening the tickets pile up without limit. And it has four cooks only because somebody guessed four. The next two lessons deal with both.

compare.title: Closing a pool in Java and Kotlin

java.title: UseDemo.java (sketch)
java.html: try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (int n = 1; n <= 10; n++) { int k = n; futures.add(pool.submit(() -> k * k)); } int total = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : futures) { total += f.get(); // must handle InterruptedException and ExecutionException } System.out.println("sum of squares 1..10 = " + total); } // close(): shutdown, then wait for every task

kotlin.title: UseDemo.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Kotlin's use {} calls ExecutorService.close() (JDK 19+), which waits for the tasks to finish. */ fun main() { val total = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> val futures = (1..10).map { n -> pool.submit<Int> { n * n } } futures.sumOf { it.get() } // get() can still throw ExecutionException; Kotlin just doesn't force a catch } println("sum of squares 1..10 = $total") }

compare.note: Both versions submit ten small sums and end in ExecutorService.close(), so the waiting is the same. Kotlin's use is its try-with-resources, and it works on a pool because ExecutorService has been AutoCloseable since JDK 19. (On older JDKs, write the shutdown idiom in a finally block.) The real difference is checked exceptions, the ones Java makes you catch or declare. Java makes you deal with InterruptedException and ExecutionException from get(). Kotlin compiles without a catch, so a failed task turns up as an exception you never planned for. Kotlin's coroutines, its own light tasks with a track of their own, can also run on a pool through asCoroutineDispatcher(). That dispatcher needs closing too, and closing it shuts the pool down.

worked.title: Close the kitchen without losing its order log

steps.say: The kitchen keeps a log file of finished orders. Four cooks (a pool of 4) cook the orders, and each one writes a line to the shared orderLog, a BufferedWriter, when its dish is done. Here is the end of main as first written. Decide what happens to orders that are still cooking when the program reaches orderLog.close().
steps.code: for (Order o : orders) pool.execute(() -> cookAndLog(o)); pool.shutdown(); orderLog.close(); // close the log file System.out.println("kitchen closed");

alt.html: for (o in orders) pool.execute { cookAndLog(o) } pool.shutdown() orderLog.close() // close the log file println("kitchen closed")

steps.say: shutdown() returned at once, so orderLog.close() ran while cooks were still cooking. Every order that finishes after that tries to write to a closed file and fails with an IOException that says Stream closed. And "kitchen closed" prints while the kitchen is still busy. Nothing waited for anything.

Wait, with a deadline. Say the building closes 10 minutes after the last order, so the cooks get 9 of them. Then we interrupt the stragglers and record what never started. The log is closed only after the pool has terminated.
steps.code: pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new orders try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish List<Runnable> unstarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt, collect the rest System.err.println(unstarted.size() + " orders never started"); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } orderLog.close(); // 4. only now

alt.html: pool.shutdown() // 1. no new orders try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish val unstarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt, collect the rest System.err.println("${unstarted.size} orders never started") pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } orderLog.close() // 4. only now

steps.say: If there's no deadline, JDK 19's try-with-resources is shorter, and it gets the order right by construction: the block can't end before the pool has terminated.
steps.code: try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (Order o : orders) pool.execute(() -> cookAndLog(o)); } // close() waits for every order orderLog.close(); System.out.println("kitchen closed");

alt.html: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> for (o in orders) pool.execute { cookAndLog(o) } } // close() waits for every order orderLog.close() println("kitchen closed")

lab.title: Build a tiny fixed pool
steps: Meet the class. TinyPool is this lesson's kitchen in code: a fixed number of worker threads, the cooks, that take tasks from one shared queue, the rail. The constructor and a few small methods are done. Run the tests once: all eight fail with UnsupportedOperationException.
Write execute: a null check, then, inside synchronized (lock), throw RejectedExecutionException if shutdown is set, otherwise queue.add(task).
Write workerLoop: take() a task, return on POISON or on InterruptedException, run the task, and count a RuntimeException in failed instead of letting it escape.
Write shutdown (under the lock: set the flag, add one POISON per worker) and awaitTermination (wait on the terminated latch).
Write shutdownNow: under the lock, set the flag, drain the queue into a list, remove the pills from it and add fresh ones. Then interrupt every worker and return the list.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them twice more.
hints: Why add pills in shutdownNow as well? A running task may swallow the interrupt. When it ends, its worker goes back to take(). Without a pill waiting there, that worker blocks forever and awaitTermination never returns true.
BlockingQueue.drainTo(list) moves everything in the queue into list in one call, in queue order.
The shutdownNow test checks that you return the very same Runnable objects, in the order they were queued. Don't wrap them.
lab.done: All eight tests in TinyPoolTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the shutdown idiom from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write static void stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace). It stops new work, waits up to grace for the backlog, interrupts stragglers, waits 5 more seconds, and handles its own interruption correctly. Then compare. Did you set the interrupt flag again?

answer.html: static void stop(ExecutorService pool, Duration grace) { pool.shutdown(); // no new tasks try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt what is still running if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { System.err.println("pool did not terminate"); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the flag for the caller } }

alt.title: stop.kt
alt.html: fun stop(pool: ExecutorService, grace: Duration) { pool.shutdown() // no new tasks try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { pool.shutdownNow() // interrupt what is still running if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { System.err.println("pool did not terminate") } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // keep the flag for the caller } }

recap: A new platform thread costs a trip to the kernel and a stack, and a thread per task has no ceiling. A pool creates a few threads once and queues the rest of the work.
Executor has one method, execute. ExecutorService adds submit, invokeAll, invokeAny and the lifecycle methods.
With execute, a failure reaches the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler. With submit, it waits inside the Future, and you see it only if you call get().
shutdown() rejects new tasks and returns at once. shutdownNow() also hands back the tasks that never started and interrupts the running ones.
Wait with awaitTermination(timeout), or with close() on JDK 19 and later, which waits with no timeout. A forgotten pool's non-daemon threads keep the JVM alive.
The limit: inside, a fixed pool is a queue plus workers looping on take(). Its queue has no end and its size is a guess, which the next two lessons fix.

explain.prompt: A friend asks what shutdown(), shutdownNow() and awaitTermination() each do, and in what order a program should call them when it has 30 seconds to stop. Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: shutdown() stops the pool from taking new tasks but lets the queued and running ones finish. It returns at once, so it only starts the stop. awaitTermination(timeout) is the waiting part: it blocks until the pool has finished everything or the time is up, and its return value tells you which. shutdownNow() is the hard stop: it takes out the tasks that never started, hands them back, and interrupts the running ones, which only works if those tasks respond to interrupts. With 30 seconds, I'd first stop taking new work, call shutdown(), wait about 20 seconds with awaitTermination, then call shutdownNow() and log what came back, wait a few more seconds, and only then close anything the tasks were still using, such as files or database connections.

deeper.html:
ThreadPoolExecutor has five run states, not three: RUNNING, SHUTDOWN, STOP, TIDYING and TERMINATED. shutdown() moves it to SHUTDOWN. shutdownNow() moves it to STOP, from either of the first two. When the queue is empty and the last worker has exited, the pool moves to TIDYING, runs the protected terminated() hook (override it to log something or release a resource), and then becomes TERMINATED. Threads blocked in awaitTermination wake only at that last step.

The state and the worker count live together in one AtomicInteger called ctl. The top 3 bits hold the state and the low 29 bits hold the count. That's why the Javadoc caps a pool at about 500 million workers: (2^29) - 1. Packing both into one number lets execute ask "still running?" and "room for one more worker?" and claim the slot with one compare-and-set, the same atomic check-and-act that the lab gets from a lock.

One more detail from the Executors Javadoc: newSingleThreadExecutor() is "guaranteed not to be reconfigurable to use additional threads", unlike newFixedThreadPool(1). The fixed pool is a plain ThreadPoolExecutor, so any code holding it can cast it and call setMaximumPoolSize. The single-thread executor is wrapped so that nobody can. If your design depends on tasks running one at a time, in order, say so with newSingleThreadExecutor().
